name: Uguisu no fun (nightingale dropping facial)

lead: Uguisu no fun is a Japanese cosmetic powder made from the droppings of the Japanese bush warbler (uguisu). It is mixed with water into a paste and applied to the face as a facial treatment.

Practitioners say it brightens skin, evens tone and helps with hyperpigmentation. Geisha reportedly used it to remove heavy white makeup and to condition the skin, and it has become a luxury spa treatment in some cities.

paras: The powder is mixed with water into a paste, massaged into the skin for a few minutes and rinsed off. Spas offer it as a treatment and some producers add rice bran for gentle exfoliation.
The mechanism is described as not entirely clear and published clinical studies were not found. Producers say the droppings are UV-sanitised, but individual sensitivity to any facial product varies.

angle.text: People use it as a facial to lighten and smooth the look of their skin. The benefits are those reported by users and spas.

lead: Uguisu no fun, meaning nightingale droppings, is a Japanese cosmetic made from the feces of the Japanese bush warbler, sometimes marketed as the geisha facial.[1]

It is used to brighten and even out skin. Proponents say it addresses hyperpigmentation and conditions skin, attributing this to urea, guanine and enzymes, although the mechanism is described as not entirely clear.[1]
infobox: Dried powder mixed into a paste

paras: Use is traced to the Heian period (794-1185), initially for removing dye from fabric and stains from silk kimono, and it became a beauty treatment in the Edo period (1603-1868).[1] Geisha reportedly used it to remove oshiroi, a white makeup that contained lead and zinc, and to whiten skin; Buddhist monks reportedly polished scalps with it.[1]

Caged birds are fed organic seeds, and droppings are collected, sanitised with ultraviolet light, dried and ground to a powder; some producers add rice bran.[1] Modern spas offer it as a facial; one New York spa reportedly charged $180 for an hour-long treatment, and Victoria Beckham has reportedly used it.[1]
Users say it whitens skin and treats uneven tone. The urea is said to retain moisture, and guanine is said to give an iridescent effect.[1]

timeline.event: Heian period: earliest reported uses on fabric.[1]
Edo period: becomes a beauty treatment.[1]
